name: The Law of Definite Proportions
statement: A pure compound always holds its elements in the same fixed proportion by mass.
statementAccent: the same fixed proportion by mass
meaning: A given chemical compound always contains its constituent elements in a fixed ratio by mass, whatever its source or how it was made. The mass fractions of each element are constant. Water made by burning hydrogen and water from a river carry the same proportions of hydrogen and oxygen. It is one of the founding laws of stoichiometry.
mechanism: Compounds form from atoms combining in small whole-number ratios. Because each atom of an element has a characteristic, near-fixed mass, a fixed ratio of atoms produces a fixed ratio of masses. This is exactly why Dalton's atomic theory explains the law: the discreteness and fixed masses of atoms make the composition of a pure compound constant. The law was, in turn, a key piece of evidence for that atomic picture.

examples.text: Water is always about eleven per cent hydrogen and eighty-nine per cent oxygen by mass, a hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio of one to eight, no matter where the water comes from or how it is made.
Sodium chloride always combines sodium and chlorine in the same fixed mass proportion, roughly thirty-nine per cent sodium to sixty-one per cent chlorine, whatever its origin.
Proust argued that copper carbonate prepared in the laboratory or found in nature always held the same fixed proportions of copper, carbon, and oxygen — the evidence that won his case.

variants.name: Daltonides and berthollides
variants.text: Kurnakov's later distinction between fixed-composition compounds, daltonides, and variable-composition solids, berthollides, named for the two rivals in the original dispute.

variants.name: The stoichiometric laws
variants.text: The trio of definite proportions, multiple proportions, and conservation of mass that, grounded in Dalton's atomism, established modern stoichiometry.

whyItMatters: It was one of the pillars on which modern chemistry was built, drawing the crucial distinction between a true compound, with fixed composition, and a mere mixture, whose proportions can vary. That distinction, and the law's role as evidence for the atomic theory, made it foundational; it remains an excellent working rule for the vast majority of ordinary compounds.

working.text: treat a pure compound as having the same mass proportions of its elements regardless of source, the basis of stoichiometric calculation.
reserve the law for pure compounds; mixtures, solutions, and alloys have variable composition and do not obey it.
allow for genuine exceptions among certain solids whose composition really does vary.

limits: The law holds excellently for ordinary molecular and ionic compounds but has real exceptions. Non-stoichiometric compounds, the berthollides, vary in composition: wustite, ideally iron oxide, is iron-deficient, with a range of compositions, and many metal oxides, sulfides, and hydrides behave similarly. Isotopes complicate the mass ratio, since natural variation in isotopic composition shifts it slightly, an effect usually negligible except for hydrogen, where heavy water differs measurably. Polymers and other extended substances are not well described by a single fixed small-integer mass ratio. So Berthollet, who lost the original dispute, was not entirely wrong.
misreadings: The law is not exceptionless: non-stoichiometric compounds genuinely vary in composition, which is why they are named after Berthollet. It applies to pure compounds, not to mixtures, solutions, or alloys, and the confusion of the two was exactly what the original controversy turned on. And it is distinct from the law of multiple proportions, which compares different compounds of the same elements rather than fixing the composition of one.
origin: Established by the French chemist Joseph Louis Proust in the 1790s, commonly dated to 1797-1799, against Claude Louis Berthollet, who held that composition could vary; Dalton's atomic theory soon after gave it a theoretical basis.
